(Tetra Tech) has prepared this biological resources evaluation report for the proposed Griffith Energy Project (Project). Griffith Energy, LLC (Griffith Energy) proposes to develop approximately 20 acres of a 102.6 acre site (approximately 95.4 acres in San Joaquin County, California and 7.2 acres of land located in Alameda County), into a battery energy storage facility. Together, the Project site and a 150-meter buffer comprise the biological study area (BSA). Biologists visited the BSA in January 2022 to conduct the following as part of the general biological survey: • Inventory of all plants and wildlife observed onsite. • Perform vegetation community mapping. • Perform a jurisdictional wetland delineation. • Assess habitat for California tiger salamander (CTS), including upland and aquatic habitat assessment and migration barrier assessment within a 1.24-mile buffer around the Project site. • Identify potential nesting habitat for Swainson’s hawk within a 0.5-mile buffer of the Project site. • Assess habitat for San Joaquin kit fox (SJKF). • Assess habitat for special-status species. • Assess habitat for nesting birds. The purpose of this biological resources evaluation report is to: • Document the methods and results of the field survey. • Summarize the existing biological resources and conditions within the Project site and vicinity. • Assess the potential presence of special-status biological resources. • Recommend additional surveys. 1.1 Project Site Location, Ecoregion, and Setting 1.1.1 Project Site Location The Project site is located along the border of San Joaquin and Alameda Counties in California (Figures 1 and 2). It is generally bound by rolling hills used for wind-energy generation, cattle grazing, and residential housing. The Diablo Mountain Range is approximately 3 to 5 miles south and west of the Project site. The nearest city is Tracy, California, which is approximately 4.5 miles east of the Project site. Interstate 580 is approximately 1 mile to the northeast and Interstate 205 is approximately 2 miles north of the Project site. The Project site is within Township 2 South, Range 4 East, Section 32 in San Joaquin and Alameda Counties. The Project site is centered at a latitude of 37.710 degrees North and longitude of -121.554 degrees West (in decimal degrees). The Project site is also in the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Midway 7.5-Minute Topographic Quadrangle Map (Figure 3). The Project property consists of two parcels with the following Assessor’s Parcel Numbers: 20910019 (San Joaquin County) and 99B-7885-2 (Alameda County) . USGS Topographic Map Biological Resources Evaluation Report Griffith Energy Project Tetra Tech, Inc. 1-5 July 2023 1.1.2 Ecoregion The Project site is located within the Great Valley Geomorphic Province, which is a broad, flat, alluvial plain about 50 miles wide and 400 miles long in the central part of California between the Sierra Nevada in the east and the Coast Ranges in the west (Jepson Flora Project [eds.] 2021). The Central Valley is composed of two valleys: 1) the northern and smaller valley, known as the Sacramento Valley, which is drained by the Sacramento River; and 2) the southern and larger valley, known as the San Joaquin Valley, which is drained by the San Joaquin River (California Department of Conservation, California Geological Survey 2002). The Project site is located within the San Joaquin Valley subregion of the Great Valley (Jepson Flora Project [eds.] 2021). 1.1.3 Land Use Based on historical aerial imagery (Google Earth©), the Project site has consisted of herbaceous vegetation and has been used for grazing since 1985. Two houses were built within the boundary of Project site between 2002 and 2003. The topography of the Project site appears unchanged throughout this period. Based on information provided by the landowner, the Project site is annually grazed by cattle. The area of the Project site within San Joaquin County is designated as agriculture and open space land (San Joaquin County Community Development Department 2013), and the portion in Alameda County is designated as an unincorporated, wind-resource area (ICF International 2010). Biological Resources Evaluation Report Griffith Energy Project Tetra Tech, Inc. 3-1 July 2023 3 LITERATURE REVIEW This section describes the study methods (literature review) used for evaluating the biological resources within the BSA and Project vicinity. A Critical Issues Analysis (CIA) was initially prepared for this Project (Tetra Tech 2021). The information in the CIA has been incorporated into the sections below as applicable. 3.1 Topography Methods The USGS 7.5-Minute Topographic Map Midway Quadrangle as well as aerial imagery were reviewed. Topography describes the physical features of an area of land. The topographic features looked at include natural landforms, aquatic features, developed lands, agricultural lands, undeveloped lands, and terrain. Natural landforms are natural physical features on the surface of the land, such as mountains, hills, and canyons. Results Site topography consists of four gently sloping hills as well as flat terrain. The Project site is used for cattle grazing and the surrounding land uses consist of agriculture, open space, and developed land. The elevational range of the Project site is approximately 300 to 500 feet above mean sea level. 3.2 Sensitive Natural Communities Methods The California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) California Natural Diversity Database (CNDDB) (CDFW 2021a) was used to identify sensitive natural communities that exist within the USGS Midway Quadrangle and surrounding quadrangles. Results The CNDDB identified one sensitive natural community, valley sink scrub, documented 5 miles northwest from the Project site in 1987. This community is still intact according to the database (CDFW 2021a). 3.3 Potential Jurisdictional Wetlands Methods The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) database (USFWS 2021), the U.S. Department of Agriculture National Resources Conservation Service (USDA NRCS) Web Soil Survey (USDA NRCS 2021), and USGS National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) (USGS 2021) were accessed to determine which areas of the Project site could contain wetland features. Results The USFWS NWI database identified one potential riverine feature within the Project boundary (USFWS 2021). The NHD identified one potential body of water in the southeast corner of the Project site (USGS 2021). Biological Resources Evaluation Report Griffith Energy Project Tetra Tech, Inc. 3-3 July 2023 Biological Resources Evaluation Report Griffith Energy Project Tetra Tech, Inc. 3-4 July 2023 3.6 Wildlife Movement Methods The Essential Connectivity Map located on CDFW’s Biogeographic and Information Observation System (BIOS) Habitat Connectivity Viewer was reviewed to determine if the Project site is located within or near a CDFW designated Natural Landscape Block (NLB) or Essential Connectivity Area (ECA) (CDFW 2021b). The Essential Connectivity Map serves to focus attention on large areas important to maintaining ecological integrity at the broadest scale. NLBs and ECAs describe habitats that provide refuges for wildlife and corridors for wildlife movement between wildlands. Results Per the BIOS Habitat Connectivity Viewer, the Project site lies within an area designated as category 4 (Conservation Planning Linkages) of CDFW’s Terrestrial Connectivity Areas of Conservation Emphasis. However, due to the broad, State-wide nature of the Essential Connectivity Map, use of macro-scale data, and its focus on connecting very large blocks of natural lands, it is unlikely that conditions specific to the Project site have been incorporated into the analysis. The Project site is within the California Bay Area Linkage Network (Penrod et al. 2013), which identifies areas that are either high quality habitat or highly permeable to wildlife movement and connects larger wildlands with smaller wildlands. The Project site is also within a San Joaquin Valley Wildlife Corridor (Huber 2006). San Joaquin Valley Wildlife Corridors connect areas of conservation opportunity to healthy, native habitats. Since the Project site is located within the designated areas described above, it has the potential to contain or function as a wildlife movement corridor. However, these designated areas also extend far beyond the boundaries of the Project site and have not incorporated conditions specific to the site into the analysis. Other factors considered when reviewing habitat connectivity of the Project site were: • Paved roads are located along the western and northern boundaries of the Project site and the entire site is surrounded by cattle fencing. • The Project site consists of a relatively small footprint that would not substantially reduce habitat connectivity in the region. The ability of wildlife to move through areas adjacent to the Project site would be unaffected. • The Project site contains small mammal burrows and foraging habitat to adequately support local wildlife species and enable movement through the site. Impacts to habitat connectivity would be evaluated during the CEQA process. Any measures required to avoid, minimize, or mitigate impacts to habitat connectivity would be proposed at that time. Biological Resources Evaluation Report Griffith Energy Project Tetra Tech, Inc. 4-1 July 2023 4 FIELD SURVEY METHODS A general biological survey was conducted on January 11 and 12, 2022. The field survey was conducted during daylight hours and not during abnormal or excessive cold, heat, wind, rain, or other inclement weather. The survey was conducted on foot and by vehicle. An Eos Arrow 100 sub-meter Global Positioning System (GPS) unit and a paired tablet running the ArcGIS Field Maps application were used to collect location and attribute data of features or species encountered. Photographs that were taken are provided in Appendix A. 4.1 Inventory of Plants and Wildlife The BSA was surveyed for special-status plant species and their habitats. Signs of wildlife, such as tracks, burrows, dens, nests, nest sites, scat, or remains were also surveyed for. Wildlife species encountered visually or audibly during the survey and wildlife sign were identified and recorded. 4.2 Vegetation Mapping Vegetation communities were mapped in accordance with the Manual of California Vegetation, Second Edition (Sawyer et al. 2009). Vegetation was mapped to the alliance level, which is defined by plant species composition and identified by the most dominant tree, shrub, or herb in the vegetation community. 4.3 Jurisdictional Wetland Delineation A jurisdictional delineation was performed within the Project site. The delineation was conducted at any potential jurisdictional wetlands and Waters of the U.S. and State, and areas potentially under CDFW jurisdiction. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) has developed standard methods and data reporting forms contained in the Interim Regional Supplement to the Corps of Engineering Wetland Delineation Manual: Arid West Region (USACE 2008), a supplement to the Corps of Engineers Wetland Delineation Manual (Environmental Laboratory 1987), to determine the presence or absence of wetlands and Waters of the U.S. The USACE methodology was used to identify wetlands and Waters of the U.S. in the Project site that are potentially subject to regulation under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act. This delineation methodology was also used to evaluate potential Waters of the State under Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB) jurisdiction. “Waters of the State” are defined by the Porter-Cologne Act as “any surface water or groundwater, including saline waters, within the boundaries of the state” (State Water Resources Control Board [SWRCB] 2019). These may include intermittent or ephemeral waters. The SWRCB and each RWQCB regulate activities in Waters of the State which include Waters of the U.S. Areas of CDFW jurisdiction were determined by the presence of a defined bed, bank, and channel, or presence of a lake or pool, and were measured to the top of bank or the edge of riparian vegetation. Sample points were taken to determine areas of potential jurisdiction and were mapped in the field using a GPS receiver with sub-meter accuracy. Field indicators were examined, and wetland data reporting forms were used to record three parameters: hydrophytic vegetation, wetland hydrology, and hydric soils. Sample points were collected for each potential jurisdictional feature when a change in any of the three wetland parameters occurred. Sample points were also collected within the feature and in associated upland to compare these areas and determine the extent of the feature. Photographs taken during the field survey are provided in Appendix A. Completed wetland data forms are provided in Appendix B. Any potential burrows/dens and burrow surrogates for BUOW, SJKF, or American badger were mapped and photographed. To assess habitat for rare plants, soil types, vegetation cover, and disturbance on the Project site were evaluated. Habitat assessments conducted for CTS, Swainson’s hawk, and SJKF are described in the subsections below. 4.4.1 California Tiger Salamander and California Red-Legged Frog To assess CTS and CRLF upland and aquatic habitat, the presence of small mammal burrows, water bodies on the project site, vegetation and debris cover, the grazing regime, and the presence of predatory and competing species were evaluated. Important CTS habitat features include ephemeral pools and a relative abundance of small mammal burrows (USFWS 2004). Methods for identification and assessment of potential CTS breeding sites in the Project vicinity is described in the subsection below. Important CRLF habitat features include shrubby or emergent riparian vegetation along still or slow-moving water at two-feet depth or greater. Habitat requirements for CRLF also include small mammal burrows or damp vegetation, such as leaf litter, for use during summer. 4.4.1.1 Assessment of Barriers to California Tiger Salamander Migration An assessment of barriers to CTS migration between the nearest known and potential breeding ponds and the Project site was conducted. Potential breeding sites were identified using aerial imagery and hydrologic spatial data from the NWI (USFWS 2021) and NHD (USGS 2021). Previously documented breeding sites were identified using search results from the CNDDB (CDFW 2021a). Each potential breeding site was visited during the survey and notes were recorded on features that may restrict the ability of CTS to access the site (e.g., roads, walls, steep slopes, trenches). Habitat data, such as water body feature type and surrounding vegetation, for each breeding site was also recorded. Paved and dirt roads are not considered as barriers to CTS migration, but high-density residential development and Interstate Highways are considered significant physical barriers (USFWS 2003). Non-lethal barriers were also taken into account. Non-lethal barriers include structures longer than 12 meters and above the recommended minimum barrier height for fencing meant to divert amphibians,12-15 inches (Langton and Clevenger 2021). Features which could facilitate access, such as culverts or small mammal burrows, were also noted. When possible, binoculars were used from vantage points to survey sites that were on private property. Notes and photographs were recorded for all accessible sites within the 1.24-miles of the Project site. 4.4.2 Swainson’s Hawk A raptor nesting habitat assessment was conducted in the Project site and surrounding 0.5-mile buffer. Aerial imagery and binoculars were used to find and survey potential trees and other features (e.g., power poles) that could be used for raptor nesting. Visual surveys for nests and perched raptors were performed. Potential Swainson’s hawk nesting features (e.g., trees, power poles) were mapped within a 0.5-mile buffer of the Project site. 4.4.3 San Joaquin Kit Fox A SJKF habitat assessment was conducted in the Project site and 150-meter buffer. Meandering transects were performed to evaluate potential denning habitat and prey availability. Potential dens and manmade features (e.g., culverts and drainage pipes) within the required size and depth range for SJKF were photographed and mapped. Observations of small mammals and the presence of small mammal burrows were used to assess the availability of prey. The presence of potential predators or competitors (e.g., large hawks, coyotes, domestic dogs) was also recorded. This riverine area was determined to be an erosional feature that was approximately 1 foot wide and 6 inches deep (Figure 5). No ponded or flowing water or evidence of standing water was observed within this feature, and it did not have a defined bed, bank, and channel. The area recorded in the NHD as a freshwater emergent wetland is the same area described in Section 5.2 as an area of cut logs and leaf litter (Figure 5). Where this feature was located, there was no depression or channel to hold water, no standing water present, and no hydrophytic vegetation. Because this area did not have any wetland characteristics, no jurisdictional delineation was conducted. The following text discusses potential jurisdiction of the erosional feature. 5.4.1 U.S. Army Corps of Engineers In April 2020, the USACE and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published the Navigable Waters Protection Rule in the Federal Register, which became effective on June 22, 2020. Following a federal district court decision on August 30, 2021, the USACE and EPA halted implementation of the Navigable Waters Protection Rule and began interpreting Waters of the U.S. consistent with the “pre-2015” regulatory regime (USACE and EPA 2021). Under the pre-2015 regulations, the onsite erosional feature is not considered a Water of the U.S. because it was an ephemeral feature, that is hydrologically isolated from other waters of the U.S. Non-navigable waters that are not relatively permanent would only have USACE jurisdiction if they have a significant nexus to a traditional navigable water. This feature did not connect to downstream traditional navigable waters. There were several factors that were considered in the conclusion that there was no significant nexus. First, there was no connection to the closest natural aquatic feature, Patterson Run, which is approximately 0.5 to 1 mile north-northwest to the Project site. Second, due to the infrequent flow, low volume, and short duration of flow, the feature on the Project site had a minimal capacity to transfer nutrients and organic carbon that support food webs. As confirmed in the field, the ditch did not have a direct physical connection to Patterson Run or any other offsite feature. Based on this evaluation, it was concluded that this feature lacks a significant nexus to traditional navigable waters. Therefore, no Section 404 Waters of the U.S. were identified within the Project site. 5.4.2 Regional Water Quality Control Board RWQCB and SWRCB Waters of the State include USACE Section 404 jurisdictional wetlands and Waters of the U.S. No areas under USACE jurisdiction were identified at the Project site. Intermittent and ephemeral surface waters may be considered jurisdictional Waters of the State, regardless of a significant nexus, but the feature on the Project site did not have a defined bed, bank, and channel and lacked hydrophytic vegetation and hydric soils. The only hydrology present was surface soil cracks due to recent rains. Therefore, no RWQCB/SWRCB Waters of the State were identified at the Project site. 5.4.3 California Department of Fish and Wildlife California Fish and Game Code, Sections 1600-1616, regulates activities that would alter the flow, bed, banks, channel, or associated riparian areas of a river, stream, or lake. CDFW jurisdiction over lakes and streams is to the top of bank, or edge of riparian vegetation as determined by edge of dripline. The onsite feature did not meet the criteria for CDFW jurisdiction since it did not have a defined bed, bank, and channel or riparian vegetation. The findings presented above are subject to verification by the USACE, RWQCB, and CDFW. These species along with their Federal status, State status, and/or California Rare Plant Rank (CRPR) are listed in Table 6. 5.5.2 California Tiger Salamander CTS is a Federally and State threatened species. This species has been previously documented several times, between 2015-2016, 3 miles from the Project site (CDFW 2021a). Ephemeral ponds lasting at least 30 days for breeding and an additional 10 weeks for larval development are necessary for successful breeding (USFWS 2004). Suitable breeding habitat consists of vernal pools, stock ponds, or other ephemeral wetlands that do not contain fish or bullfrog predators. Emergent or submerged vegetation or debris is necessary for egg attachment. Suitable upland habitat includes grazed annual grassland no further than 1.24 miles from a known or potential breeding site (USFWS 2003). Networks of small mammal burrows in upland habitat are necessary for CTS estivation (Pittman 2005). Because the Project site has many California ground squirrel burrows (Figure 6) but no ephemeral sources of water that could provide CTS breeding habitat, the Project site is potential upland habitat only. Although CTS larvae have been recorded in cattle troughs (Alvarez et al. 2021), the concrete cattle trough found onsite is unlikely to be used as breeding habitat because there was no bank or slope for CTS to access the water in the trough and CTS cannot climb over structures greater than 15 inches (Langton 2021). Three California slender salamanders (Batrachoseps attenuates) were observed during the survey at the surface of the soil under the cover of logs, indicating that soils may hold enough moisture during the dry season to support estivating amphibians. 5.5.2.1 Assessment of Barriers to California Tiger Salamander Migration An assessment was conducted to analyze potential barriers to CTS migration between potential breeding ponds/pools and the Project site. The nearest known breeding site is 2 miles to the southwest of the Project site; migration from this area was not considered in the analysis because it is further than 1.24 miles from the Project site. A total of six aquatic features within 1.24 miles of the Project site were visited. Three additional aquatic features that could serve as potential breeding pools were identified within 1.24 miles but could not be visited because they are on private land. Out of the six aquatic features visited, only one potential CTS breeding pond was identified, which was 1 mile from the Project site (Pool 1, Photo 10, Appendix A). A map of potential breeding pools and barriers is provided in Figure 7. Two types of potential CTS barriers were identified within the 1.24-mile assessment radius: high-density development and steep slopes without passages. A previous study conducted by USGS indicates that migrating CTS can only successfully cross through a physical barrier if there are passages at least every 40 meters along the barrier (Brehme et al. 2021). Slopes greater than 14 degrees are considered barriers to CTS movement (Pittman 2005); the only exception would be if passages are present. Cattle fencing and most paved roads are not considered barriers to upland dispersal (USFWS 2003). Table 5 describes specific barriers and the pools that would be affected. The Project site is not located within CRLF Critical Habitat; however, the Project site provides potential estivation habitat in the form of a perennial cattle trough and California ground squirrel burrows. Ideally, breeding habitat has emergent vegetation and still or slow-moving water at 2-foot depth or deeper. Water must last a minimum of 4-6 months for breeding and metamorphosis. This species is also known to use stock ponds and cattle troughs for breeding (Hemingway 2005). Ideal upland habitat are creek, seeps, or freshwater-spring corridors with riparian vegetation, but this species can occupy different types of upland habitats, including annual grassland (e.g., Avena spp. – Bromus spp. herbaceous semi-natural alliance). CRLF upland habitat is typically located within 1 mile of a breeding site. The Project site is not within a 1-mile distance of known CRLF breeding habitat. Although there are no known breeding ponds within a 1-mile distance from the Project site (CDFW 2021a), there are two potential breeding ponds within 1 mile of the site. One pond is covered in bulrush (Scripus sp.) and is located 120 feet north of Via Nicolo Road, approximately 1 mile east of the Project site (Pool 5, Figure 7). If this pond holds water, then it could provide potential breeding habitat for CRLF. Pool 1 may also provide potential breeding habitat for CRLF but is located at the maximum dispersal distance for this species of 1 mile (Figure 7). Based on the NWI search and aerial imagery, there are at least seven additional cattle ponds that hold water through August, approximately 1.5 miles to the west and southwest of the Project site. The Project site is also surrounded by four ephemeral creeks within 0.5 to 1 mile which could facilitate safe dispersal for CRLF from these potential breeding sites to the Project site. CNDDB records have previously documented one breeding pond 1.5 miles northwest of the Project site in 2004 (CDFW 2021a). CNDDB records also document this species 2 miles from the project site in 1996, 2001, 2004, and 2008 (CDFW 2021a). In addition, within 3 to 5 miles from the Project site, the CNDDB has records of eight breeding ponds (CDFW 2021a). About half of these sites are within Corral Hollow Creek; however, dispersal from this Creek to the Project site is unlikely because CRLF would have to migrate over a steep elevation Biological Resources Evaluation Report Griffith Energy Project Tetra Tech, Inc. 5-12 July 2023 gain (approximately 500 feet) and this species does not appear to use slopes greater than 30-40 degrees (USFWS 2000). Considering these factors, the Project site may provide upland habitat that could be used by CRLF. 5.5.4 Special-Status Reptiles California glossy snake, San Joaquin coachwhip, and coast horned lizard are each a CDFW Species of Special Concern. These reptiles inhabit grassland habitats (e.g., Avena spp. – Bromus spp. herbaceous semi-natural alliance). California glossy snake is a primarily fossorial species and is found in areas with sandy and loose soils. The most recent sighting was 3 miles from the Project site in 2010 (CDFW 2021a). The closest occurrence is one mile north of the Project site in 1994 (CDFW 2021a). The San Joaquin coachwhip inhabits open, valley grassland habitats with sparse shrub cover. They require small mammal burrows for egg-laying and refuge from extreme temperatures. The most recent sighting was 5 miles from the Project site and the nearest sighting from the Project site was 0.5 mile in 1996 (CDFW 2021a). The coast horned lizard frequents a wide variety of habitats but is most common in lowlands along sandy washes with scattered low bushes. The most recent sighting of this species was 5 miles from the Project site in 2003 (CDFW 2021a). Due to the lack of sandy substrates for burrowing and suitable prey base, the coast horned lizard does not have habitat on the Project site. The Project site provides potential habitat for the California glossy snake and San Joaquin coachwhip. 5.5.5 Burrowing Owl BUOW is a CDFW Species of Special Concern. BUOWs breed and live in burrows and use coastal prairie, coastal scrub, Great Basin grassland, Great Basin scrub, Mojavean Desert scrub, Sonoran Desert scrub, and valley and foothill grassland habitats as well as agricultural areas or any open dry area with low vegetation. The Project site is in the known distributional range of the BUOW, and the site contains potentially suitable BUOW habitat due to low-growing vegetation and abundance of small mammals found during the field survey. In addition, this species has been previously documented on the Project site in June 2007 (CDFW 2021a). A total of eight potentially suitable burrows, likely dug by California ground squirrels, and one burrow surrogate (i.e., culvert) were found within the Project site during the survey. These burrows had entrance diameters greater than approximately 4 inches and were above 60 inches in depth, and therefore, were considered potentially suitable for BUOW. No BUOW sign was observed at the potential burrows or burrow surrogates. 5.5.6 Swainson’s Hawk Swainson’s hawk is listed as a State threatened species and the San Joaquin Valley hosts the majority of California’s breeding pairs. This species nests primarily in riparian or isolated trees between March 1 and September 15. Although no Swainson’s hawks were observed during the general biological survey, adult Swainson’s hawks are not expected to be in the San Joaquin Valley in January. Trees within the Project boundary are not suitable nesting habitat for Swainson’s hawk or other raptors. Although trees in the BSA met the height and foliage cover requirements for Swainson’s hawk nesting and are considered potential habitat, these residential areas undergo high levels of disturbance (e.g., vehicle traffic, dogs, human activity). Adjacent areas in the 0.5-mile buffer undergo comparably less disturbance. The potential Swainson’s hawk and raptor nesting habitat within the Project site and 0.5-mile buffer consisted of over ten transmission towers and numerous 8 to 10-foot trees of various species in residential areas and in stands along Patterson Run. Federally listed endangered: an animal or plant in danger of extinction within the foreseeable future throughout all or a significant portion of its range. State listed endangered: “endangered species” means a native species or subspecies of a bird, mammal, fish, amphibian, reptile, or plant which is in serious danger of becoming extinct throughout all, or a significant portion, of its range due to one or more causes, including loss of habitat, change in habitat, overexploitation, predation, competition, or disease (Fish and Game Code § 2062). State listed threatened: "threatened species" means a native species or subspecies of a bird, mammal, fish, amphibian, reptile, or plant that, although not presently threatened with extinction, is likely to become an endangered species in the foreseeable future in the absence of special protection and management efforts (Fish and Game Code § 2067). BCC = Federal Bird of Conservation Concern: The Birds of Conservation Concern 2021 List identifies migratory and non-migratory bird species (beyond those already designated as Federally threatened or endangered) that represent the USFWS’ highest conservation priorities. FP = CDFW Fully Protected: the classification of “Fully Protected” was California’s initial effort in the 1960's to identify and provide additional protection to those animals that were rare or faced possible extinction. Most Fully Protected species have also been listed as threatened or endangered species under the California Endangered Species Act. Fully Protected species may not be taken or possessed at any time and no licenses or permits may be issued for their take except for necessary scientific research, relocation of bird species for the protection of livestock, or if they are a covered species in a Natural Community Conservation Plan (Fish and Game Code §§ 3511, 4700, 5050, and 5515). CRPR = California Rare Plant Rank: 1B = Plants rare, threatened, or endangered in California and elsewhere. 0.1 = Seriously threatened in California (over 80% of occurrences threatened / high degree and immediacy of threat). Biological Resources Evaluation Report Griffith Energy Project Tetra Tech, Inc 6-1 July 2023 6 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS The Project site is within the planning area for both the San Joaquin County Multi-Species Habitat Conservation and Open Space Plan (SJMSCP) and East Alameda County Conservation Strategy (EACCS). The SJMSCP plan area covers all of San Joaquin County except for federally owned lands. A majority (approximately 90%) of the Project site is within the SJMSCP plan area along the western boundary of San Joaquin County. The current Project site plans avoid Alameda County with the exception of the gen-tie line and access road. The eastern boundary of the EACCS plan area follows the Alameda County line. A small portion (approximately 10%) of the Project site is within the EACCS plan area along the eastern boundary of Alameda County. Additional coordination with the agencies (e.g., CDFW, San Joaquin and Alameda Counties) is recommended to determine if both the SJMSCP and EACCS apply to the Project site or if only one would be used. The SJMSCP (San Joaquin County 2000) and EACCS (ICF International 2010) provide measures to avoid, minimize, and mitigate impacts on special-status species and sensitive habitats. Both of these plans have been finalized. Projects with anticipated impacts to special-status species that are within San Joaquin County are eligible for incidental take coverage under the SJMSCP and would not require incidental take permits for SJMSCP Covered Species. Conversely, the EACCS is a regional conservation strategy that only provides guidelines and recommended avoidance, minimization, and mitigation measures for focal species and habitats. The EACCS does not provide incidental take permits for special-status species, as is the case in a Habitat Conservation Plan such as the SJMSCP, but rather serves as guidance for project-level permits. Therefore, work within Alameda County would still require project-level incidental take permits if impacts to special-status species are anticipated. Recommendations from the SJMSCP and EACCS have been incorporated into Section 6.1. All recommendations within this report are preliminary and will be refined during the CEQA process as more details about the Project design and schedule are determined. 6.1 Additional Survey Recommendations 6.1.1 Rare Plants Two rare plants have the potential to occur on the Project site. Therefore, rare plant surveys are recommended within the Project site. To capture the blooming period for all potential rare plants that could occur, two rare plant surveys are recommended. The first rare plant survey should be conducted in March to April and the second in July to November. The following rare plant species with medium or high potential to occur will be surveyed for during each rare plant survey: • First Rare Plant Survey (March to April): caper-fruited tropidocarpum (Tropidocarpum capparideum). • Second Rare Plant Survey (July to November): big tarplant (Blepharizonia plumosa). 6.1.2 California Tiger Salamander The Project is not within Critical Habitat of CTS or within 5 miles of an area designated as Critical Habitat (USFWS ECOS 2021). Project applicants have the following two options for CTS (ICF International 2010): 1. Assume CTS presence and mitigate. Mitigation would likely entail habitat enhancement/conservation easement on a protected property since there are no agency-approved mitigation banks in the area. Biological Resources Evaluation Report Griffith Energy Project Tetra Tech, Inc 6-2 July 2023 2. Have a USFWS and CDFW-approved biologist conduct surveys using the 2003 Interim Guidance to determine if CTS are present (USFWS 2003). If CTS are present, the project would proceed with avoidance, minimization, and mitigation measures. If no CTS are present, then no mitigation is necessary, but avoidance and minimization measures may still be required by the agencies since suitable upland habitat is present. Therefore, it is recommended to assume presence of CTS and mitigate rather than conducting protocol surveys. No CTS were found during the general biological survey; however, CTS would be overwintering in small mammal burrows at the time of the survey. The Project site contains suitable habitat for CTS and is within the CTS distributional range. If presence is not assumed, to determine the presence/absence of this species on the Project site, a protocol survey would be required (USFWS 2003). A CTS site assessment would be submitted to the USFWS. Upon reviewing the results from the site assessment, USFWS is likely to determine that the Project site contains upland habitat only. At sites that only contain upland habitat and at least one potential breeding pool within 1.24 miles, a one-year drift fence study would be required in the fall and winter, between two consecutive seasons of aquatic larval surveys, to support a negative finding. 6.1.3 Burrowing Owl The SJMSCP does not specifically require BUOW protocol surveys. As allowed under the SJMSCP, this species may be addressed by implementing pre-construction surveys and avoidance buffers (i.e., 75 meters) during construction if nesting owls are found (San Joaquin County 2000). The EACCS recommends that the CDFW protocol survey is implemented (CDFW 2012). The following summarizes the recommendations and timing for protocol-level BUOW surveys: • BUOW protocol surveys require that 100 percent of a project site and 150-meter buffer be thoroughly surveyed by walking transects spaced no more than 20 meters apart to look for potential suitable burrows. • After the burrow transect survey is completed, four breeding season surveys and census of BUOW must be conducted prior to beginning work activities. Nesting season surveys must be conducted between February 15 and July 15, with the first survey occurring between February 15 and April 15 and the last survey occurring between June 15 and July 15. These surveys occur from two hours before sunset to one hour after or from one hour before to two hours after sunrise. • One winter survey must be conducted between December 1 and January 31 if BUOW are not found during the nesting season survey. After the surveys are completed, a report documenting the methods and results must be submitted to the CDFW. After it is determined which of the two plans applies to the Project, that plan should be followed for BUOW as described above. 6.1.4 Additional Requirements Pre-construction surveys are recommended prior to ground disturbance or vegetation clearance to avoid impacts to special-status species that have potential to occur on the Project site. Pre-construction surveys would occur 7 to 30 days prior to construction activities (e.g. equipment staging, potholing) depending on species. Pre-construction surveys would be needed for CRLF, Swainson’s hawk, nesting birds (including raptors), SJKF, and American badger. Pre-construction surveys for SJKF are recommended to include the use of motion-activated cameras, which would be setup and monitored 14 to 30 days prior to construction activities. The recommended density of camera placement is equal to about two camera stations in an average SJKF home range, or about 1 camera station per 2.9 square kilometers (Westall and Cypher 2017). Minimization measures for these special-status reptiles would be included in the CEQA document and reviewed by regulating agencies. If special-status species are observed during any protocol or pre-construction surveys, avoidance buffers specific to that species would be implemented and a biological monitor may be required during ground-disturbance activities. Additional consultations with agencies may also be required, depending on which species is observed. Griffith Energy, LLC (Griffith Energy) proposes to develop approximately 20 acres of a 132-acre site into a battery energy storage facility. A majority of the Project site is located in San Joaquin County, California and a small western portion of the Project site is located in Alameda County (Figure 1). The Project site of 132 acres was surveyed for rare plants in 2022. Tetra Tech previously conducted a literature search and a general biological survey in January 2022 at the proposed Project site (Tetra Tech 2022). Based on the general biological survey results and the habitats found onsite, an assessment of rare plants that could occur onsite was performed (Tetra Tech 2022). The Biological Resources Evaluation Report recommended conducting rare plant surveys for caper-fruited tropidocarpum (Tropidocarpum capparideum) and big tarplant (Blepharizonia plumosa) based on this assessment (Tetra Tech 2022). Both of these species have a California Rare Plant Rank (CRPR) of 1B.1, which indicates that they are rare, threatened, or endangered in California and elsewhere and are considered seriously threatened in California. One rare plant survey was conducted for caper-fruited tropidocarpum in March 2022 and a second survey was conducted for big tarplant in September 2022. The purpose of this rare plant survey report is to document the methods and results of the rare plant surveys. 1.1 Project Site Location, Ecoregion, and Land Use 1.1.1 Project Site Location The Project site is located along the border of San Joaquin and Alameda Counties in California (Figures 1 and 2). It is generally bound by rolling hills used for wind-energy generation, cattle grazing, and residential housing. The Diablo Mountain Range is between 3 and 5 miles south and west of the Project site. The nearest city is Tracy, California, which is 4.5 miles east of the Project site. Interstate 580 is approximately 1 mile to the northeast and Interstate 205 is approximately 2 miles north of the Project site. The Project site is within Township 2 South, Range 4 East, Section 32 in San Joaquin and Alameda Counties. The Project site is centered at a latitude of 37.710 degrees North and longitude of -121.554 degrees West (in decimal degrees). The Project site is also in the U.S. Geological Survey Midway 7.5-Minute Topographic Quadrangle Map (Figure 3). The Project property consists of two parcels with the following Assessor’s Parcel Numbers: 20910019 (San Joaquin County) and 99B-7885-2 (Alameda County). 1.1.2 Ecoregion The Project site is located within the Great Valley Geomorphic Province, which is a broad, flat, alluvial plain about 50 miles wide and 400 miles long in the central part of California between the Sierra Nevada in the east and the Coast Ranges in the west (Jepson Flora Project [eds.] 2021). The Central Valley is composed of two valleys: 1) the northern and smaller valley, known as the Sacramento Valley, which is drained by the Sacramento River; and 2) the southern and larger valley, known as the San Joaquin Valley, which is drained by the San Joaquin River (California Department of Rare Plant Survey Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 2 July 2023 Conservation, California Geological Survey 2002). The Project site is located within the San Joaquin Valley subregion of the Great Valley (Jepson Flora Project [eds.] 2022). 1.1.3 Land Use Based on historical aerial imagery (Google Earth©), the Project site has consisted of herbaceous vegetation and has been used for grazing since 1985. Three houses were built within the Project site between 1993 and 2003. The topography of the Project site appears unchanged throughout this period and is comprised of four hills with slopes of 25 percent or less. The Project site is annually grazed by cattle and also has three onsite houses with ornamental landscaping. The area of the Project site within San Joaquin County is designated as agriculture and open space land (San Joaquin County Community Development Department 2013), and the portion in Alameda County is designated as an unincorporated, wind-resource area (ICF International 2010). Surrounding land uses consist of agriculture, open space, and developed land. The elevational range of the Project site is approximately 300 to 500 feet above mean sea level. Rare Plant Survey Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 7 July 2023 3.0 SURVEY METHODS A literature review was conducted that included the California Department of Fish and Wildlife California Natural Diversity Database (CNDDB) RareFind 5 online database and the California Native Plant Society online Inventory of Rare and Endangered Plants of California (CDFW 2022). Based on the literature review and general biological survey results, two rare plants were determined to have potential to occur on the Project site: big tarplant and caper-fruited tropidocarpum (CDFW 2022; Tetra Tech 2022). Previous CNDDB records of big tarplant and caper-fruited tropidocarpum are located outside the Project site; big tarplant was previously found approximately 25 feet to the west of the Project site in 2003 and caper-fruited tropidocarpum was found approximately 120 feet to the northwest of the Project site in 1987 (CDFW 2022, CNPS 2021). Caper-fruited tropidocarpum blooms from March to April and big tarplant blooms from July to November. Therefore, two rare plant surveys were conducted on the Project site to capture the blooming periods of the rare plant species with the potential to occur onsite. The first rare plant survey for caper-fruited tropidocarpum was conducted in March 2022. The second rare plant survey for big tarplant was conducted in September 2022. Two biologists surveyed the entire Project site during each survey by walking meandering transects throughout the Project site. Transects were spaced 30 meters apart to ensure 100 percent visual coverage of the Project site. All plant species found onsite were identified and recorded. The surveys were conducted during daylight hours and clear conditions at temperatures of approximately 60-80 degrees Fahrenheit. Any rare plant populations found onsite were mapped using a sub-meter accuracy Global Positioning System unit and individuals were counted. Photographs that were taken during the surveys are provided in Appendix A. Rare Plant Survey Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 8 July 2023 4.0 SURVEY RESULTS The Project site is undeveloped other than three small residential areas. All undeveloped areas of the site consisted of Avena spp. – Bromus spp. herbaceous semi-natural alliance. Cattle were actively grazing the site during the rare plant survey in March 2022. Grazing on the site has greatly reduced the cover of non-native grasses such as slender wild oat (Avena barbata) and bromes (Bromus spp.) as compared to the surrounding non-grazed areas offsite. Most of the site cover was comprised of non-native redstem filaree (Erodium cicutarium) with some small patches of non-native cheeseweed (Malva parviflora), black mustard (Brassica nigra), and greenstem filaree (Erodium moschatum). By September 2022, vegetation cover in undeveloped areas of the site was comprised almost entirely of dead non-native annuals such as filarees and mustards with some sprouts of Russian thistle (Salsola sp.). Non-native olive trees (Olea europaea) and pepper trees (Schinus sp.) and ornamental pine trees (Pinus sp.) were found in residential areas. No sensitive natural communities were found during the rare plant surveys. CNDDB records from 2003 documented an existing offsite population of big tarplant (CRPR 1B.1) approximately 25 feet west of the Project site, across Midway Road (CDFW 2022). This existing offsite population was observed during the September 2022 survey since it occurs directly across from the Project site. Multiple 1.6 meters tall big tarplant and many other shorter big tarplant were observed in this offsite area. Similar to the Project site, this area consisted of Avena spp. – Bromus spp. herbaceous semi-natural alliance, but had higher cover of non-native grasses than the site and less intensive cattle grazing. One rare plant species, big tarplant, was found on the western portion of the Project site during the September 2022 rare plant survey. This species was found onsite in erosional areas where soil was disturbed and supported less herbaceous cover. This species is generally known to occur in grasslands and disturbed areas such as burned areas. Specimens of this plant were sent to Dr. Bruce Baldwin of the Jepson Herbarium at University of California, Berkeley and it was verified to be the rare big tarplant by Dr. Baldwin (Baldwin 2022). Two populations of big tarplant were observed within the Project site. The specific locations and boundaries of these populations are shown in Figure 4. Population 1 consisted of 395 individuals and was 0.09 acres in size. Population 2 consisted of 167 individuals and was 0.15 acres in size. Both populations occurred in ephemeral erosional features that had higher cover of bare soil relative to other areas of the Project site. Although this species can grow to over 1.8 meters tall, individuals on the Project site were stunted, likely due to disturbance by cattle grazing, and were up to 0.6 meters tall. Herbivory by cows was observed on some big tarplant individuals. Yellow star-thistle (Centaurea solstitialis), a species rated “High” by the California Invasive Plant Council (Cal-IPC) was found onsite. Yellow star-thistle was predominantly found along fencelines and in areas with stormwater runoff such as near roads. Species rated High by the Cal-IPC have severe ecological impacts on physical processes, plant and animal communities, and vegetation structure. Their reproductive biology and other attributes are conducive to moderate to high rates of dispersal and establishment, and most are widely distributed ecologically. Rare Plant Survey Results Rare Plant Survey Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 12 July 2023 5.0 CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS The rare plant surveys were conducted during the appropriate blooming periods for the rare plants (caper-fruited tropidocarpum and big tarplant) that could potentially occur onsite. One rare plant species, big tarplant (CRPR 1B.1), was found on the Project site during the surveys. In addition, the survey results are sufficient to determine absence of caper-fruited tropidocarpum on the Project site. It is recommended that Project impacts avoid the populations of big tarplant if feasible (Figure 4). While big tarplant is not federally or state listed, impacts to this species must be evaluated in the California Environmental Quality Act document and mitigation measures would be required if it cannot be avoided. The following preliminary measures are recommended for this species: • A qualified biologist will flag a minimum no-disturbance buffer of 10 feet around big tarplant populations in the field, and if feasible, these areas will be avoided during construction. To delineate the areas of avoidance, a pre-construction survey would be required during the blooming period for this species (July to November) during the blooming period that occurs prior to the start of construction. For example, if construction were planned to start in June 2024, the area would be surveyed between July and November 2023 and those results would be used to determine the extent of the population areas. • For big tarplant areas that cannot be avoided, a restoration/enhancement plan for impacts to big tarplant will be prepared. The plan will include the following components as needed: figures showing the restored areas; invasive plant species management procedures; topsoil and/or seed collection and dispersal protocols; maintenance requirements; monitoring and performance standards; and reporting requirements. Temporary impacts (i.e., impacts in areas that would be restored to natural conditions) may be mitigated by salvaging topsoil during ground disturbance, storing the soil onsite and protecting it from weed seed dispersal, and then returning the soil horizon to its original profile to keep seeds at the appropriate soil depth. Permanent impacts (i.e., impacts in areas that would not be restored to natural conditions) may be mitigated by enhancing other big tarplant habitat within or outside the Project site, through seed collection and planting and invasive plant control. Topsoil would not be salvaged in the case of permanent impacts, and other habitat enhancement methods would be used, such as seed collection and dispersal, in other non-impacted locations. The actual areas impacted will be mapped post-construction to quantify the amount of big tarplant impacted. Location: Project Site West Aspect: N/A Appendices Griffith Energy Storage Project Tetra Tech / SCH 2022120675 Draft Environmental Impact Report August 2023 Appendix E-3 Biological Resources Technical Memorandum Memorandum 1 July 2023 Technical Memorandum for 2023 Site Visit at NextEra Griffith Energy Date: July 28, 2023 Attention: Craig Lawrence, Patti Murphy Company: NextEra Energy Resources Prepared by: Tetra Tech 1.0 INTRODUCTION This Memorandum summarizes the methods and results of a site visit that was conducted on June 7, 2023 at the proposed Griffith Energy Project site. Comments from MIG, Inc. (MIG), San Joaquin County’s third-party reviewer of the Draft Environmental Impact Report (EIR), were received on May 19, 2023 and July 21, 2023. Multiple comments on the Biological Resources section of the Draft EIR referenced the presence of an ephemeral pond in the southwest portion of the Project property after a historically high rainfall year. The purpose of the site visit was to document current conditions at the Project site to inform the applicant’s response to MIG’s comments. A detailed impacts analysis will be performed in the EIR. 2.0 METHODS One biologist visited the Project site on June 7, 2023. The following bullets outline the tasks that were performed during the site visit: • Map and assess ephemeral pond in southeast portion of property. Assess habitat in this area for western spadefoot (Spea hammondii), longhorn fairy shrimp (Branchinecta longiantenna), vernal pool fairy shrimp (Branchinecta lynchi), California tiger salamander (Ambystoma californiense, CTS), and California red-legged frog (Rana draytonii). Conduct a jurisdictional delineation. • Evaluate offsite location where West Patterson Pass Road passes under the railroad and assess for potential barriers to CTS wildlife movement. • Check standing water location west of Midway Road for potential to support vernal pool invertebrates. • Map shallow ditch that runs along the southern side of West Patterson Pass Road within 150-meter buffer. The biologist recorded notes, mapped locations on a tablet synced with a global positioning system (GPS) and took photographs. Memorandum 2 July 2023 3.0 RESULTS 3.1 Ephemeral Pond The ephemeral pond was observed in the southeast portion of the property (Figure 1 in Attachment A). The pond appeared to have recently receded, based on the presence of surface soil cracks, but standing water was still present at a depth of approximately 1 to 2 feet deep. The water was turbid and murky, and the soil was a silty clay color of 10YR 3/1. Deep soil cracks were present where the water had receded. Cattle tracks surrounded the pond; cattle were observed elsewhere within the Project property during the site visit. Two debris piles containing cut wood were observed; one is located next to the pond, and one was located in the pond (the general location is shown in Figure 1). Two species of common amphibians were observed to be inhabiting the pond and directly adjacent area, specifically: California toad (Anaxyrus boreas halophilus) and Sierran treefrog (Pseudacris sierra). No tadpoles or fairy shrimp were observed in the water. Photographs of the ephemeral pond are included in Attachment B. 3.1.1 Special-status Species The pond was evaluated for its potential to support special-status species, such as CTS, western spadefoot, and vernal pool invertebrates such as the longhorn fairy shrimp and vernal pool fairy shrimp. If water is present, the ephemeral pond has the potential to support breeding habitat for the CTS and western spadefoot. The pond would not support breeding California red-legged frog due to the lack of emergent vegetation. However, it is infrequently ponded as shown in historic aerial imagery and was not observed during previous Tetra Tech surveys in January, March, and September 2022. This pond is likely only present during high rainfall years, such as the 2022-2023 historically high rainfall year. During a review of available aerial imagery from 1937 to 2022, there was no evidence of ponding water. This pond likely only holds water seasonally during high rainfall years and is typically dry; therefore, the likelihood of longhorn fairy shrimp and vernal pool fairy shrimp presence in this pond is low. Branchiopod cysts can persist in soil substrate for decades, but generally require recurring ponding to continue their lifecycle. The EIR will include an analysis of the Project’s potential impacts to CTS, western spadefoot, California red-legged frog, and vernal pool invertebrates. Measures will be proposed to mitigate Project impacts. Although the ephemeral pond is outside of the Project footprint, it is approximately 40 feet away from the Project footprint boundary and has the potential to be impacted by indirect effects. 3.1.2 Jurisdictional Delineation The pond was evaluated for hydrophytic vegetation, hydric soils, and wetland hydrology per the Interim Regional Supplement to the Corps of Engineering Wetland Delineation Manual: Arid West Region (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers [USACE] 2008), a supplement to the Corps of Engineers Wetland Delineation Manual (Environmental Laboratory 1987), to determine the presence or absence of wetlands and Waters of the U.S. that are potentially subject to regulation under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act. This delineation methodology was also used to evaluate potential Waters of the State under Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB) jurisdiction. “Waters of the State” are Memorandum 3 July 2023 defined by the Porter-Cologne Act as “any surface water or groundwater, including saline waters, within the boundaries of the state” (State Water Resources Control Board [SWRCB] 2019). These may include intermittent or ephemeral waters. The ephemeral pond was also assessed for presence of a lake or pool, measured to the top of bank or edge of riparian vegetation, that is subject to California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) jurisdiction under Section 1602 of the Fish and Game Code. The pond is mostly unvegetated, with approximately one percent cover of sprouting doveweed (Croton setigerus) and black mustard (Brassica nigra) along the edges. No wetland vegetation was observed. Vegetation on the adjacent, gradual slopes next to the ephemeral pond include non-native grasses, such as wall barley (Hordeum murinum), rye grass (Festuca perennis), brome (Bromus spp.), and California burclover (Medicago polymorpha). Wetland hydrology was observed due to the presence of surface water which was approximately 1 to 2 feet deep and surface soil cracks where the surface water has evaporated. Hydric soil was observed due to the presence of redox dark surface (F6) and redox depressions (F8) in each surface layer (0 to 2 inches; 2 to 6 inches; and 6 to 15 inches). The soil was primarily clay/loam with 10 YR, v4/c1 and 10 YR, v3/c1 coloration. The ephemeral pond is not a USACE wetlands due to the lack of hydrophytic vegetation. This feature is not a Waters of the U.S. because it is hydrologically isolated. However, it is likely jurisdictional to the RWQCB and CDFW. 3.2 Railroad Underpass Along West Patterson Pass Road There is a 20-foot-long paved road under the railroad tracks bridge (Attachment B). There are steep dirt berms on the east and wide side of the road. Consistent vehicle traffic was noted along the road. CTS may be able to climb the dirt berm, cross the paved road with vehicle traffic, then use the road under the railroad tracks bridge to access nearby grassland areas. Therefore, the Union Pacific railroad is not a complete barrier to CTS migration, but rather is a partial barrier. 3.3 Standing Water West of Midway Road The standing water observed west of Midway Road within 150-meters of the site has the potential to support vernal pool invertebrates. Aerial imagery indicates that this feature holds water regularly, although ephemerally. However, no standing water was observed in this feature during June 2023, which may indicate that standing water is not present long enough for the entire vernal pool invertebrate lifecycle. Regardless, this area is outside of the Project footprint on the opposite of a paved roadway and will not be impacted directly or indirectly by proposed activities. 3.4 Ditch South of West Patterson Pass Road A shallow ditch that is located on the south side of West Patterson Pass Road within the 150-meter buffer was observed by Tetra Tech during 2022 surveys and by MIG during their April 2023 site visit. This ditch was mapped by Tetra Tech during the June 2023 site visit and has been added to Figure 1 in Attachment A. This ditch ranges from 1 to 8 feet wide and was mostly dry, except for standing water observed at one location north of the railroad and next to the road near the end of the feature. The Memorandum 4 July 2023 ditch is mostly unvegetated with edges of non-native grasses, including brome, slender wild oat (Avena barbata), rye grass, and wall barley as well as yellow star-thistle (Centaurea solstitialis), and poison hemlock (Conium maculatum). 3.5 Other Special-status Species with Potential to Occur 3.5.1 Crotch’s Bumble Bee Crotch’s bumble bee is a candidate for listing under the California Endangered Species Act. Although no bumble bees of any species were observed during the site visit or previous Project biological surveys and there are no known occurrences recorded near the Project Property, floral resources (foraging habitat), burrows and crevices (nesting habitat), and leaf litter (overwintering habitat) were observed. However, the site is routinely grazed and trampled by cattle, which likely interferes with the Crotch’s bumble bee habitat requirements and reduces habitat suitability (Xerces Society et al. 2018). 3.5.2 White-tailed Kite The white-tailed kite is a fully protected species by CDFW. Potential white-tailed kite nesting habitat includes trees located adjacent to the Project Property to the north and northwest. Numerous 8 to 10-foot-tall trees of various species in residential areas have the potential to provide nesting habitat. The open grassland within the Project Property provides potential foraging habitat for white-tailed kites. 3.5.3 Grasshopper Sparrow Tetra Tech notes that MIG observed a grasshopper sparrow, a CDFW Species of Special Concern, by sight and sound during their April 2023 site visit. 4.0 CONCLUSION The Project Site design changed after preparation of the Biological Resources Evaluation Report and Rare Plant Survey Report (Tetra Tech 2022a, 2022b). The Draft EIR analyzes potential impacts to biological resources based on the current Project design. Due to the observation of an ephemeral pond in spring 2023 after a historically high rainfall year, additional special-status species, such as western spadefoot and vernal pool invertebrates, have the potential to occur at the Project Property. Although the ephemeral pond will not be directly impacted by proposed Project activities, there is the potential for indirect effects to the pond itself (which may be jurisdictional to RWQCB and CDFW) and the special-status species that may inhabit the pond. Therefore, the EIR has been revised to analyze these potential effects and include mitigation measures. Additional species, including the Crotch’s bumble bee and white-tailed kite, will be discussed in the EIR and their impacts from the proposed Project activities will be analyzed. Measures will be proposed to mitigate potential impacts to these species. Memorandum 5 July 2023 5.0 REFERENCES Environmental Laboratory. 1987. Corps of Engineers Wetlands Delineation Manual. The site includes Grazing Land and Farmland of Local Importance, as classified by the California Department of Conservation. 1.2 Acoustical Metrics and Terminology All sounds originate with a source, whether it is a human voice, motor vehicles on a roadway, or a combustion turbine. Energy is required to produce sound and this sound energy is transmitted through the air in the form of sound waves – tiny, quick oscillations of pressure just above and just below atmospheric pressure. These oscillations, or sound pressures, impinge on the ear, creating the sound we hear. A sound source is defined by a sound power level (abbreviated “LW”), which is independent of any external factors. By definition, sound power is the rate at which acoustical energy is radiated outward and is expressed in units of watts. A source sound power level cannot be measured directly. It is calculated from measurements of sound intensity or sound pressure at a given distance from the source outside the acoustic and geometric near-field. A sound pressure level (abbreviated “LP”) is a measure of the sound wave fluctuation at a given receiver location and can be obtained through the use of a microphone or calculated from information about the source sound power level and the surrounding environment. The sound pressure level in decibels (dB) is the logarithm of the ratio of the sound pressure of the source to the reference sound pressure of 20 microPascals (μPa), multiplied by 20. The range of sound pressures that can be detected by a person with normal hearing is very wide, ranging from about 20 μPa for very faint sounds at the threshold of hearing, to nearly 10 million μPa for extremely loud sounds such as a jet during take-off at a distance of 300 feet. Acoustic Terms and Definitions Term Definition Noise Typically defined as unwanted sound. This word adds the subjective response of humans to the physical phenomenon of sound. It is commonly used when negative effects on people are known to occur. Sound Pressure Level (LP) Pressure fluctuations in a medium. Sound pressure is measured in dB referenced to 20 μPa, the approximate threshold of human perception to sound at 1,000 Hz. Sound Power Level (LW) The total acoustic power of a noise source measured in dB referenced to picowatts (one trillionth of a watt). Noise specifications are provided by equipment manufacturers as sound power as it is independent of the environment in which it is located. A sound level meter does not directly measure sound power. Equivalent Sound Level (Leq) The Leq is the continuous equivalent sound level, defined as the single sound pressure level that, if constant over the stated measurement period, would contain the same sound energy as the actual monitored sound that is fluctuating in level over the measurement period. A-Weighted Decibel (dBA) Environmental sound is typically composed of acoustic energy across all frequencies. To compensate for the auditory frequency response of the human ear, an A-weighting filter is commonly used for describing environmental sound levels. Sound levels that are A-weighted are presented as dBA in this report. Unweighted Decibels (dBL) Unweighted sound levels are referred to as linear. Linear decibels are used to determine a sound’s tonality and to engineer solutions to reduce or control noise as techniques are different for low and high frequency noise. Sound levels that are linear are presented as dBL in this report. Propagation and Attenuation Propagation is the decrease in amplitude of an acoustic signal due to geometric spreading losses with increased distance from the source. Additional sound attenuation factors include air absorption, terrain effects, sound interaction with the ground, diffraction of sound around objects and topographical features, foliage, and meteorological conditions including wind velocity, temperature, humidity, and atmospheric conditions. Acoustical Analysis Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 4 August 2023 1.3 Vibration Metrics and Terminology Vibration is an oscillatory motion that is described in terms of displacement, velocity, or acceleration. Velocity is the most common descriptor used when evaluating human perception or structural damage. Velocity represents the instantaneous speed of movement and more accurately describes the response of humans, buildings, and equipment to vibrations. Peak-Particle-Velocity (PPV) and root mean square velocity are typical metrics used to describe vibration levels in units of inches per second in the United States. However, to evaluate annoyance to humans, the vibration dB (VdB) notation is commonly used. The decibel notation acts to compress the range of numbers required to describe vibration. In the United States, the accepted velocity reference for converting to dB is 1x10-6 inches per second. The abbreviation “VdB” is used for vibration dB to reduce the potential for confusion with sound decibels. In contrast to airborne noise, ground-borne vibration is not an everyday occurrence for humans. The background vibration velocity levels within residential areas are usually 50 VdB or lower, which is well below the human perception threshold of approximately 65 VdB. However, human response to vibration is not usually significant unless the vibration exceeds 70 VdB. For a significant impact to occur, vibration levels must exceed 72 VdB during frequent events, 75 VdB for occasional events, and 80 VdB during infrequent events (Federal Transit Administration 2006). Outdoor sources that generate perceptible ground-borne vibrations are typically construction equipment, steel-wheeled trains, and traffic on rough roadways. Effects of noise at various levels can include interference with sleep, concentration, and communication, and can cause physiological and psychological stress and hearing loss. Given these effects, some land uses are considered more sensitive to ambient noise levels than others. In general, residences, schools, hotels, hospitals, and nursing homes are considered to be the most sensitive to noise. These locations are referred to as noise sensitive areas (NSAs). Places such as churches, libraries, and cemeteries, where people tend to pray, study, and/or contemplate also are NSAs. Commercial and industrial uses are considered the least noise sensitive. Details regarding each set of requirements are provided below. 2.1 California Environmental Quality Act CEQA requires that significant environmental impacts be identified and that such impacts be eliminated or mitigated to the extent feasible. Appendix G of the CEQA Statutes and Guidelines (State Clearing House, Office of Planning and Research and the Natural Resources Agency, 2023) sets forth a series of suggested thresholds for determining a potentially significant impact. Under the thresholds suggested in Appendix G, the proposed Project could be considered to have significant noise and vibration impacts if it results in one or more of the following: a) Generation of substantial temporary or permanent increase in ambient noise levels in the vicinity of the project in excess of standards established in the local general plan or noise ordinance, or in other applicable local, state, or federal standards? b) Generation of excessive groundborne vibration or groundborne noise level? c) For a project located within the vicinity of a private airstrip or an airport land use plan or, where such a plan had not been adopted, within two miles of a public airport or public use airport, would the project expose people residing or working in the project area to excessive noise levels? 2.2 San Joaquin County Ordinance Code San Joaquin County regulates noise through Chapter 9-1025 within the County Ordinance Code. Per Table 9-1025.9 Part II of the San Joaquin County Ordinance Code, exterior noise at noise sensitive areas is limited to 50 dBA during the daytime (7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m.) and 45 dBA during the nighttime (10:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m.). Further, maximum noise levels are not permitted to exceed 70 dBA during the daytime and 65 dBA during nighttime. Noise sources associated with construction are exempt from these maximum noise levels, provided construction does not occur before 6:00 a.m. or after 9:00 p.m. on any day. The USEPA methodology distinguishes between type of construction and construction stage. The basic model assumed spherical wave divergence from a point source located at the center of the Project site to each receptor structure. Acoustical Analysis Report Griffith Energy Storage Project 13 August 2023 6.0 OPERATIONAL NOISE This section describes the model utilized for the assessment; input assumptions used to calculate noise levels due to the Project’s normal operation; a conceptual noise mitigation strategy, and the results of the noise impact analysis. 6.1 Noise Prediction Model The Cadna-A® computer noise model was used to calculate sound pressure levels from the operation of the Project equipment in the vicinity of the Project site. An industry standard, Cadna-A® was developed by DataKustik GmbH to provide an estimate of sound levels at distances from sources of known emission. It is used by acousticians and acoustic engineers due to the capability to accurately describe noise emission and propagation from complex facilities consisting of various equipment types like the Project and in most cases, yields conservative results of operational noise levels in the surrounding community. The current ISO standard for outdoor sound propagation, ISO 9613 Part 2 – “Attenuation of Sound during Propagation Outdoors,” was used within Cadna-A (ISO 1996). The method described in this standard calculates sound attenuation under weather conditions that are favorable for sound propagation, such as for downwind propagation or atmospheric inversion, conditions which are typically considered worst-case. The calculation of sound propagation from source to receiver locations consists of full octave band sound frequency algorithms, which incorporate the following physical effects: • Geometric spreading wave divergence; • Reflection from surfaces; • Atmospheric absorption at 10 degrees Celsius and 70 percent relative humidity; • Screening by topography and obstacles; • The effects of terrain features including relative elevations of noise sources; • Sound power levels from stationary and mobile sources; • The locations of noise-sensitive land use types; • Intervening objects including buildings and barrier walls, to the extent included in the design; • Ground effects due to areas of pavement and unpaved ground; • Sound power at multiple frequencies; • Source directivity factors; • Multiple noise sources and source type (point, area, and/or line); and • Averaging predicted sound levels over a given time. Cadna-A allows for three basic types of sound sources to be introduced into the model: point, line, and area sources. Each noise-radiating element was modeled based on its noise emission pattern. Larger dimensional sources such as the transformers were modeled as area sources. This was accomplished by evaluating the additional VMT caused by construction and operations. 2.3.1 Vehicle Miles Traveled The VMT metric is project-based and is implemented to help quantify traffic induced by construction and operations. The VMT metric is used to align effects on traffic with greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. VMT is presented as a time-dependent value, i.e., the number of additional VMT per week during construction and operations, as well as a total VMT value for the entire Project. The California Natural Resources Traffic Impact Study Griffith Energy Storage Project 6 February 2023 Agency adopted changes to the CEQA identifying VMT as “the most appropriate metric to evaluate a project’s transportation impacts…Thus, to achieve the State’s long-term climate goals, California needs to reduce per capita VMT.” The VMT values calculated should be compared to a jurisdictionally determined threshold of significance that ultimately dictates whether a project’s traffic impacts are significant and require mitigation or are a less than significant impact. San Joaquin County has not yet developed a threshold of significance for VMT, so in lieu of that the criteria as stated in the Technical Advisory on Evaluating Transportation Impacts in CEQA (CEQA 2018) would apply: The VMT metric can support the three statutory goals: “the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, the development of multimodal transportation networks, and a diversity of land uses.” (Pub. Resources Code, § 21099, subd. (b)(1)) However, in order for it to promote and support all three, lead agencies should select a significance threshold that aligns with state law on all three. State law concerning the development of multimodal transportation networks and diversity of land uses requires planning for and prioritizing increases in complete streets and infill development but does not mandate a particular depth of implementation that could translate into a particular threshold of significance. Meanwhile, the State has clear quantitative targets for GHG emissions reduction set forth in law and based on scientific consensus, and the depth of VMT reduction needed to achieve those targets has been quantified. Tying VMT thresholds to GHG reduction also supports the two other statutory goals. Therefore, to ensure adequate analysis of transportation impacts, OPR [Office of Planning and Research] recommends using quantitative VMT thresholds linked to GHG reduction targets when methods exist to do so.
