Traffic Impact Study Griffith Energy Storage Project 10 February 2023 5.0 CONCLUSIONS 5.1 SIGNIFICANCE OF IMPACTS 5.1.1 Vehicle Miles Traveled As noted in Section 1.3.1, there is no established threshold of significance for VMT in San Joaquin County. Since no quantitative, qualitative, or performance level is identified, the significance of 847,667 additional miles traveled must be evaluated based on the three guidance criteria from the CEQA Technical Advisory, and based on the following CEQA criteria, the Project is a less than significant impact for VMT: Reduction of GHG Emissions. The Project is a battery energy storage system facility and the chief aim of constructing such facilities is to increase local energy storage capacity. This Project would support the state policies necessary to meet the California renewable energy standards. California has proceeded to advance energy storage uses to support the grid, including the passage of AB 2514, as well as the resulting California Public Utilities Commission decision for energy procurement targets for each of the investor-owned utilities. The proposed Project would address the limitations of the electrical grid by the increasing demand for renewable energy. Layering energy storage systems into the energy grid improves grid reliability and makes it more resilient to disturbances and peaks in energy demand. The Project and other energy storage systems are used to supply power during brief disturbances, reduce outages and associated impacts to the community, and substitute for certain large footprint transmission and disruption upgrades. Additionally, Griffith conducted an Air Quality and Greenhouse Gas Technical Report for San Joaquin County which concluded a “less than significant impact” for both construction and operations emissions. The GHG technical report identified a quantitative threshold of significance for GHG emissions. The analysis included in that report accounted for construction traffic emissions to determine the total emissions for the Project. Using this definitive quantitative metric yielded a “less than significant impact.” Based on this conclusion a threshold value for VMT would likely be much higher than the Project generated VMT. This assertion is in line with the fact that the guidance for conducting VMT analysis originated with GHG emissions reduction regulations and goals and the guidance states “OPR recommends using quantitative VMT thresholds linked to GHG reduction targets when methods exist to do so.” Diversity of Land Use. Diversity of land use is a more difficult criteria to quantify for a comparative analysis. According to CEQA (2018), “State law concerning the development of multimodal transportation networks and diversity of land uses requires planning for and prioritizing increases in complete streets and infill development but does not mandate a particular depth of implementation that could translate into a particular threshold of significance.” The Project would diversify land use by changing the current use from undeveloped cropland grazing land to renewable energy storage. While the Project would increase the VMT from undeveloped to developed conditions, nearly all of the VMT are added during a relatively short construction time window. The expected facility maintenance would generate infrequent and light traffic during operations, and it is anticipated that eventually maintenance visits would be reduced to once a month or less and not impact peak hour traffic. Development of the Project would therefore support California’s statutory energy goals—reduction of GHGs through development of a storage facility for renewable energy, development of multimodal transportation networks, and a diversity of land uses. Development of Multimodal Transportation networks. This CEQA guidance criteria is not relevant to the Project. Per California Water Code Section 10910(a), a Water Supply Assessment (WSA) is required for a project for which an environmental impact report, negative declaration, or mitigated negative declaration will be prepared for the purposes of CEQA compliance. California Water Code Section 10912(a)(5) defines a project as “A proposed industrial manufacturing, or processing plant, or industrial park planned to house more than 1,000 persons, occupying more than 40 acers of land, or having more than 650,000 square feet of floor area.” The Griffith Energy Storage Project (Project) falls under this description of a project which requires a Water Supply Assessment. Water Supply Assessment Griffith Energy Storage Project 4 February 2023 1.0 PROJECT DESCRIPTION The Project is a proposed energy storage facility housing lithium-ion batteries totaling 400-megawatts of energy on a 106-acre property of land in San Joaquin County. The Project property is approximately 0.9 miles southwest of Interstate 580 and approximately 5 miles southwest of the City of Tracy, directly east to the Pacific Gas and Electric’s Tesla Substation. The energy storage facility would interconnect at the Tesla Substation immediately adjacent to the site in Alameda County via a 230-kilovolt interconnection generation tie (gen-tie) line. The Project would substantially increase energy storage capacity and address limitations of the electrical energy grid by increasing the efficacy of renewable energy. This Project and other energy storage systems are used to supply power during brief disturbances, reduce outages and associated impacts to the community, and substitute for certain large footprint transmission upgrades. Construction of the Project is anticipated to last approximately 12-months, plus 3 months for commissioning, with an estimated 10,000,000 gallons of non-potable water (approximately 30.7 acre-feet) needed for dust suppression, soil compaction, and other construction related purposes. During the Project operation and maintenance phase, the expected maintenance would generate little worker traffic and no heavy equipment would be utilized during normal operation. No permanent sanitary facilities would be required during operations. Fire protection service is expected to be provided by the Tracy Rural Fire District. The project site is approximately 3 miles west of the Tracy Rural Fire District Fire Station 94. Water Supply Assessment Griffith Energy Storage Project 5 February 2023 2.0 SUPPLY AND DEMAND ANALYSIS The WSA assesses if the demand associated with a project is available. The Project is estimated to require 10,000,000 total gallons of water (30.7 acre-feet) for construction use for a 12-month duration, plus 3 months of Project commissioning. That volume of water is equal to roughly 30 gallons per minute continuously for 12 months of construction use. One existing domestic well is located within the Project site. Per historic boring reports the well is 200 feet deep with the static water level depth at 32 feet. Downhole video surveys and a pumping test will be needed to confirm these values, the condition of the well, and if rehabilitation of the well will be needed prior to use. There is no public water system that provides water to the Project site, but the Project site is adjacent to the City of Tracy which has a public water system. The expectation is that the construction contractor may choose to haul water from the City of Tracy. This analysis includes both groundwater sources as well as public water supply sources from the City of Tracy. 2.1 SAN JOAQUIN RIVER HYDROLOGY REGION (TRACY SUBBASIN) The Project site is located within the Tracy Subbasin (Basin 5-022.15) of the San Joaquin River Hydrologic Region. Per the California Groundwater Update 2020 (Bulletin 118) the San Joaquin River Hydrological Region covers 15,200 square miles in Central California and provides nearly 4 million acre-feet per year of water to the area. The California Department of Water Resources (DWR) has identified the basin as a medium priority basin and therefore requires a Groundwater Sustainability Plan (GSP) pursuant to the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) (DWR 2019). SGMA requires medium- and high-priority basins to develop groundwater sustainability agencies (GSAs), develop GSPs, and manage groundwater for long-term sustainability. The Tracy Subbasin GSP was finalized in 2021 (GEI 2021) and will be updated every 5 years as additional information for the subbasin becomes available. The GSP identifies sustainability indicators for the subbasin, defines significant and undesirable results, minimum thresholds, and measures objectives that will be used to guide and define sustainable conditions and overall groundwater management goals within a 20-year period (GEI 2021). The GSP describes the six agencies throughout the subbasin (GSAs) that are responsible for sustainably managing groundwater in the subbasin, with each GSA having jurisdiction within their respective areas. Key components for defining sustainable conditions include water quality and groundwater level monitoring and monitoring of land subsidence via satellite-based-radar measurements. The GSP also provides technical information used to develop water budgets under historical and current conditions and under future use conditions with climate change consideration. The water budgets were developed using a state- developed model for the entire Central Valley. The water budgets show a surplus for the historic conditions and a deficit for future conditions with climate change. The GSP presents management actions for the subbasin to resolve deficits predicted by the model-based future groundwater budget. The management actions include one project that can resolve the deficit that includes reducing groundwater pumping by 1,000 AFY. There are also two supplemental projects: one project that benefits the Upper aquifer by reducing pumping by up to 3,000 acre-feet per year (AFY) and a second project that can increase recharge to the Lower aquifer by up to 3,000 AFY (GEI 2021). The largest inflow component is deep percolation and pumping is the largest outflow component, constituting of 47 percent of the total outflow. The resulting average surplus for the projected water budget is 4,806 AFY (GEI 2021). The Project requires only 30.7 acre-feet, so there is ample water supply from the Tracy Subbasin.
